```{python}
#| include: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from statsforecast import StatsForecast
from statsforecast.models import (AutoETS, Holt, HoltWinters, SeasonalNaive,
                                  SimpleExponentialSmoothingOptimized)
from utilsforecast.losses import mase as mase_loss

from coursekit import datasets as D
from coursekit import plotting as P
from coursekit import scoring

P.use_course_style()

spine = D.spine()
H = 24
train, test = D.train_test(spine, h=H)

# --- the three teaching steps, on the same 24-month holdout Day 2 used -----
steps = StatsForecast(
    models=[SimpleExponentialSmoothingOptimized(alias="SES"),
            Holt(season_length=12, alias="Holt"),
            HoltWinters(season_length=12, alias="HoltWinters")],
    freq=D.FREQ, n_jobs=1)
fc_steps = steps.forecast(df=train, h=H)

# The three steps are not course models -- they are never scored, they are one
# story told in three slides -- so they carry their own colours rather than
# borrowing from MODEL_PALETTE.
STEP_COLORS = [P.BLUE, P.GREEN, P.AMBER]

# --- what AutoETS picks on the full spine, and the states it learned -------
auto = StatsForecast(models=[AutoETS(season_length=12)], freq=D.FREQ, n_jobs=1)
auto.fit(df=spine)
ets = auto.fitted_[0, 0].model_
par = np.asarray(ets["par"])
ALPHA, GAMMA = float(par[0]), float(par[2])
METHOD = ets["method"]
states = P.ets_states(ets, spine["ds"])

# --- the AICc search, six candidates, as a distance from the winner -------
CANDIDATES = [("ANN", False), ("AAN", False), ("ANA", False),
              ("AAA", False), ("MNA", False), ("MAA", False)]
aicc = {}
for spec, damped in CANDIDATES:
    f = StatsForecast(
        models=[AutoETS(season_length=12, model=spec, damped=damped)],
        freq=D.FREQ, n_jobs=1)
    f.fit(df=spine)
    tag = f"ETS({spec[0]},{spec[1]}{'d' if damped else ''},{spec[2]})"
    aicc[tag] = float(f.fitted_[0, 0].model_["aicc"])
best_aicc = min(aicc.values())
d_aicc = {k: v - best_aicc for k, v in
          sorted(aicc.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1])}

# --- damped against undamped, five years out ------------------------------
damp = StatsForecast(
    models=[AutoETS(season_length=12, model="AAN", alias="AAN"),
            AutoETS(season_length=12, model="AAN", damped=True, alias="AAdN")],
    freq=D.FREQ, n_jobs=1)
fc_damp = damp.forecast(df=spine, h=60)

# --- and then the Day 2 harness, unchanged --------------------------------
DAY3 = ["SeasonalNaive", "AutoETS"]
LABELS = {"SeasonalNaive": "Seasonal naive", "AutoETS": "ETS"}
cvsf = StatsForecast(
    models=[SeasonalNaive(season_length=12), AutoETS(season_length=12)],
    freq=D.FREQ, n_jobs=1)
cv = cvsf.cross_validation(df=spine, h=12, step_size=12, n_windows=8,
                           level=scoring.LEVELS)
score = {m: scoring.score_cv(cv, m, spine) for m in DAY3}

# The same two models on the single 24-month window Day 2 used, and fold by
# fold, so slide 28 can show the gap against the spread it sits inside.
fc24 = cvsf.forecast(df=train, h=H, level=scoring.LEVELS)
merged24 = test.merge(fc24, on=["unique_id", "ds"])
single_mase = mase_loss(merged24, models=DAY3, seasonality=12,
                        train_df=train)[DAY3].iloc[0].to_dict()
per_window = pd.DataFrame([
    mase_loss(g.drop(columns=["cutoff"]), models=DAY3, seasonality=12,
              train_df=spine[spine["ds"] <= cut])[DAY3].iloc[0]
    for cut, g in cv.groupby("cutoff")
]).reset_index(drop=True)
width80 = {m: float((cv[f"{m}-hi-80"] - cv[f"{m}-lo-80"]).mean()) for m in DAY3}
cover80 = {m: score[m]["coverage_80"] for m in DAY3}
crps = {m: score[m]["crps"] for m in DAY3}
mase = {m: score[m]["mase"] for m in DAY3}
```

- **Part D**: the family those three steps belong to, and how it picks a member

:::

Seasonal naive, **MASE 1.18**, **scaled CRPS 0.031**, over eight rolling folds.
Its residuals fail Ljung-Box at $p \approx 10^{-240}$, so it is beatable.
:::

::: {.notes}
Open by putting yesterday's last slide back up in words. They left with a
a scoring harness they wrote themselves and a seasonal naive on top of
everything it measured, at MASE 1.18 and scaled CRPS 0.031. And they left with the reason to keep going: those
residuals are nowhere near white noise, so there is structure in this series
that none of the five benchmarks captured.

Today is one model, taught properly, and then one framework that runs a dozen
of them for you. The order matters: by the time the framework appears this
afternoon, every model inside it is one they have either built or watched get
built.

Set the expectation about the result honestly, because it is coming in Part E
and it is not a landslide. ETS will beat the floor on the point forecast by
about half a percent and lose to it on the distribution. That is a normal
result in this field, and diagnosing it is the whole exercise.
:::

# A. A forecast is a weighted average {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #00C9A7)"}

Ch 8.1 · Simple exponential smoothing

## Your benchmarks are two ends of one dial

::: {.flowrow}
[[Naive]{.flowtitle}[all the weight on $y_T$]{.flownote}]{.flownode .coral}
[[somewhere in between]{.flowtitle}[recent counts more, old still counts]{.flownote}]{.flownode .teal}
[[Mean]{.flowtitle}[equal weight on every $y_t$]{.flownote}]{.flownode .purple}
:::

. . .

The naive forecast says the last observation is all that matters. The mean says
a point from 1982 matters exactly as much as last month. Neither is what you
believe about a real series.

::: {.notes}
This is the slide that makes exponential smoothing feel inevitable rather than
invented. Both of yesterday's simplest benchmarks are weighted averages of the
history. They just sit at opposite extremes of the same dial.

Ask the room which one is closer to right for the takeaway food series. Most
will say the naive, and they are right, which is exactly why the seasonal naive
was yesterday's best benchmark. But nobody actually believes that only December
2018 carries information about December 2019.

The obvious repair is a weighted average where recent observations count more
and the weight fades as you go back. That is the whole idea, and it has a name.
:::

## Simple exponential smoothing is the dial between them

$$\hat{y}_{T+1|T} = \alpha y_T + \alpha(1-\alpha) y_{T-1} + \alpha(1-\alpha)^2 y_{T-2} + \cdots$$

Every past observation gets a weight. The weights shrink geometrically as you
go back, and they sum to 1.

. . .

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**$\alpha$ near 1**

Fast to react. Almost the naive forecast.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**$\alpha$ near 0**

Slow and smooth. Approaches the mean.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
One parameter, alpha, between 0 and 1. It is the smoothing parameter, and it
sets how fast the weight decays as you walk backwards through the history.

Point at the two columns and connect them to the previous slide: alpha equal to
1 puts a weight of exactly 1 on the last observation and zero on everything
else, which is the naive forecast. Push alpha towards 0 and the weights flatten
out towards the mean.

The word "exponential" in the name is the geometric decay, nothing more
exotic. If anyone asks why the weights sum to 1, that is the geometric series
alpha times the sum of (1 minus alpha) to the j, which is exactly 1.
:::

## Every past observation keeps a weight that fades

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
P.smoothing_weights_plot(
    alphas=(0.2, 0.5, 0.8), n_lags=16, figsize=(9, 4.6),
    title="Weight on each past observation, for three values of $\\alpha$")
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
This is the picture worth remembering from Part A. Three dials, three decay
curves. The annotated number on each curve is the weight the forecast puts on
the most recent observation, which is alpha itself.

Walk one curve. At alpha 0.8 the last observation gets 0.8, the one before it
0.16, and by four months back the weight is under one percent: this forecast
has essentially forgotten last year. At alpha 0.2 the weight is still 0.05 at
lag seven, so a year-old observation is still pulling on today's forecast.

The point to land: nothing is ever discarded. Exponential smoothing has no
window and no cutoff. Every observation the series ever had is still in the
forecast, with a weight that has faded.
:::

## The same model, written as a state you update

Two lines, and the second one is the whole model:

$$\hat{y}_{t+h|t} = \ell_t \qquad\text{(forecast)}$$
$$\ell_t = \alpha y_t + (1-\alpha)\ell_{t-1} \qquad\text{(level)}$$

. . .

::: {.cardbox .teal}
$\ell_t$ is the **state**: what the model believes the series is worth right
now. Each new observation nudges it. The forecast is just the state, held flat.
:::

::: {.notes}
Same model, different algebra. Instead of an infinite sum, one number that gets
updated. Substitute the level equation into itself a few times and the infinite
weighted sum comes back out, so these are the same object.

This form is the one that scales. The level equation says: take a step from
where you were towards what you just saw, and alpha is the size of that step.
Every model for the rest of the day is this pattern with more states.

The word state is worth saying out loud here, because the family this belongs
to is called state space models, and by Part D that name should feel earned
rather than imposed.
:::

## $\alpha$ is fitted, not chosen by hand

Pick the $\alpha$ and the starting level $\ell_0$ that minimize the sum of
squared one-step errors on the training data:

$$\text{SSE} = \sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(y_t - \hat{y}_{t|t-1}\right)^2$$

. . .

```python
from statsforecast.models import SimpleExponentialSmoothingOptimized
StatsForecast(models=[SimpleExponentialSmoothingOptimized()], freq="MS")
```

On the spine the optimizer lands on $\alpha \approx `{python} f"{ALPHA:.2f}"`$.

::: {.notes}
Nobody tunes alpha by hand. It is estimated the same way a regression
coefficient is: write down the one-step errors on the training data, square
them, add them up, and let an optimizer find the alpha and the starting level
that make the total smallest.

Two things get estimated, not one. The initial level l-zero has to come from
somewhere, and the honest answer is that it is a parameter too.

This matters for a reason that shows up in Part D: because there is a fitting
criterion, models can be compared. Hold that thought.
:::

## SES on its own gives you a flat line

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
P.forecast_overlay(
    train, fc_steps, ["SES"], labels={"SES": "SES"}, colors=[STEP_COLORS[0]],
    actual=test, history_tail=60, ncols=3, figsize=(10, 3.4),
    title="Simple exponential smoothing, 24 months out",
    ylabel="turnover ($M)")
plt.show()
```

::: {.cardbox .coral}
One state, and it is a level. There is nothing in this model that knows the
series is growing, and nothing that knows about December.
:::

::: {.notes}
Here is the result, and it is deliberately disappointing. A flat line just
above 355, against a holdout that climbs and swings.

Do not treat this as a failure of the method. It is a correct forecast from a
model with exactly one state. A level, updated month by month, extrapolates as
a horizontal line, because a level has no direction.

That is the honest motivation for the next two segments. The series has a trend
and it has a season. Give the model a state for each and watch the line pick up
the shape. Two more states, two more slides.
:::

# B. Trend: a second state {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #FF7A5C)"}

Ch 8.2 · Holt's linear trend, and damping it

## A second state gives the forecast a slope

$$\hat{y}_{t+h|t} = \ell_t + h b_t$$
$$\ell_t = \alpha y_t + (1-\alpha)(\ell_{t-1} + b_{t-1})$$
$$b_t = \beta^*(\ell_t - \ell_{t-1}) + (1-\beta^*) b_{t-1}$$

. . .

The level equation is the same as before, with the slope folded into what it
expects. The new line is the same update pattern applied to the slope itself.

::: {.notes}
Read the three lines in order and point at what changed. The forecast is no
longer flat: it is the level plus h steps of slope. The level update now starts
from where the trend said it would be, not from where it was. And the third
line is the level equation's twin, applied to the slope.

Beta-star is a second smoothing parameter with the same meaning as alpha: how
fast does the model revise its belief about the slope when the data disagrees.
It is fitted alongside alpha and the two initial states.

The pattern is the thing to notice. Every state in this family is updated by
the same move: a weighted step from what you believed towards what you just
saw.
:::

## Holt adds a slope but not a December

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
P.forecast_overlay(
    train, fc_steps, ["SES", "Holt"], labels={"SES": "SES", "Holt": "Holt"},
    colors=STEP_COLORS[:2], actual=test, history_tail=60, ncols=3,
    figsize=(10, 3.4),
    title="Adding a trend state tilts the forecast", ylabel="turnover ($M)")
plt.show()
```

::: {.cardbox .coral}
Better, and still wrong in an obvious way. Two states cannot represent twelve
months that behave differently from each other.
:::

::: {.notes}
The line now rises, which is progress you can see. Over 24 months it climbs
from about 356 to about 373, which is roughly the right slope for this series.

And it is still a straight line through a series that visibly swings by 30
percent between February and December. The residuals from this model would fail
every diagnostic in yesterday's lecture, for a reason the picture already gives
away.

Two states means two things remembered. Nothing here knows what month it is.
:::

## Extrapolate a straight line far enough and it lies

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
P.forecast_overlay(
    spine, fc_damp, ["AAN", "AAdN"],
    labels={"AAN": "linear trend", "AAdN": "damped trend"},
    colors=[P.BLUE, P.AMBER], history_tail=96, ncols=3, figsize=(10, 3.4),
    title="Five years out, the damped forecast flattens",
    ylabel="turnover ($M)")
plt.show()
```

At $h = 60$ the two disagree by about
`{python} f"{float(fc_damp['AAN'].iloc[-1] - fc_damp['AAdN'].iloc[-1]):.0f}"`
units, on a series whose last observation was
`{python} f"{float(spine['y'].iloc[-1]):.0f}"`.

::: {.notes}
Empirically, forecasts that extrapolate a constant slope forever are too
optimistic at long horizons. Hyndman's damped trend is the standard repair and
it is one extra parameter.

The damping parameter phi sits between 0 and 1 and multiplies the slope at
every step out, so the contributions form a geometric series that converges.
The forecast approaches a horizontal asymptote instead of running off the top
of the chart.

Point at the gap at the right edge. Five years out, the undamped line has added
38 units that the damped one has not. Neither is verified here, and that is the
point: nothing in the training data can tell you which is right five years out,
so the conservative one is the better default.
:::

## Damping is a parameter, not a decision

::: {.incremental}
- $\phi = 1$ recovers the plain linear trend, so damping costs nothing to allow
- $\phi$ is fitted with everything else, usually between 0.8 and 0.98
- Below about 0.8 the damping is so strong the trend barely survives one year
- In the notation coming in Part D, this model is written **ETS(A,Ad,N)**
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-note}
## On this series, damping loses
Damping the trend makes the fit *worse* on the spine by the criterion in Part D.
The room where it wins is long horizons on noisy trends, which is most of them.
:::

::: {.notes}
The reason to allow damping rather than argue about it is that phi equal to 1
is the undamped model, so a fitted phi can always fall back to it. Letting the
data choose costs one parameter.

Be straight about the callout. On this series the automatic search will reject
damping, and it will reject the trend state altogether, which is Part D's
surprise. Damping is still worth teaching, because the room will forecast
series that are noisier and horizons that are longer than this one, and it is
the standard fix in that setting.

The little d in the middle letter is worth flagging now so the notation lands
softly in twenty minutes.
:::

# C. Seasonality: the third state {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #9B8EC0)"}

Ch 8.3 · Holt-Winters

## The third state holds one value per month

$$\hat{y}_{t+h|t} = \ell_t + h b_t + s_{t+h-m(k+1)}$$
$$s_t = \gamma(y_t - \ell_{t-1} - b_{t-1}) + (1-\gamma)s_{t-m}$$

$m = 12$ here, and the seasonal state is a set of $m$ values that each get
updated once a year, when their month comes round again.

. . .

::: {.cardbox .purple}
Three states, three smoothing parameters: $\alpha$ for the level, $\beta^*$ for
the slope, $\gamma$ for the season. All fitted together.
:::

::: {.notes}
The seasonal state is different in kind from the other two, and it is worth
being explicit. There are twelve of them. Each January updates the January
state, each February the February state, and each one is refreshed once per
year rather than once per month.

The subscript arithmetic in the forecast equation is doing exactly that
bookkeeping: it reaches back to the most recent estimate for the month you are
forecasting. Do not spend more than a sentence on the k in that expression; it
just counts complete years.

Gamma is the third smoothing parameter and it answers a question worth asking
out loud: how much should one unusual December change what we believe about
Decembers?
:::

## Additive or multiplicative is a real choice

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Additive season**

$y_t = \ell_t + s_t$

December adds a fixed number of units, whatever the level is.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Multiplicative season**

$y_t = \ell_t \times s_t$

December is a fixed *percentage* above the level.
:::
::::

. . .

::: {.callout-important}
## Which one the spine wants
Its swings grew from about $\pm 2$ units in 1982 to about $\pm 55$ in 2018,
while the level grew by the same kind of factor. That is multiplicative
behaviour, and Part D shows the two ways to handle it.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the choice Day 1 already made them look at, in different clothes. When
they log-transformed this series in lecture 2, the reason was that the seasonal
swings grow with the level. Same observation, now a model decision.

The numbers in the callout are read off the fitted seasonal state, which is on
screen two slides from now, so this is a promise the deck keeps.

There are two ways out and the course teaches both: model the seasonality as
multiplicative, or transform the data until the seasonality is additive. Part D
does that pair properly. For now, the point is only that assuming additive
without looking is a decision, and usually a wrong one on retail data.
:::

## Holt-Winters finally has the right shape

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
P.forecast_overlay(
    train, fc_steps, ["SES", "Holt", "HoltWinters"],
    labels={"SES": "SES", "Holt": "Holt", "HoltWinters": "Holt-Winters"},
    colors=STEP_COLORS, actual=test, history_tail=60, ncols=3,
    figsize=(10, 4.8),
    title="Three states: level, slope, season", ylabel="turnover ($M)")
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Three slides, three models, one series. Flat, then tilted, then the right
shape. This is the arc of Part A to C in one picture, and it is worth pausing
on before the family notation arrives.

Compare the Holt-Winters line against the dashed holdout. It has the December
peaks and the February troughs in the right places and roughly the right size.
It is not perfect and it does not need to be.

If someone asks whether this beats the seasonal naive: good question, hold it
for Part E, because answering it properly needs eight folds and not this
chart.
:::

## You already built this by hand on Day 2

::: {.flowrow}
[[STL + drift]{.flowtitle}[yesterday]{.flownote}]{.flownode .navy}
[[Split the season off]{.flowtitle}[STL decides]{.flownote}]{.flownode .coral}
[[Pin drift]{.flowtitle}[your choice]{.flownote}]{.flownode .coral}
[[Pin seasonal naive]{.flowtitle}[your choice]{.flownote}]{.flownode .coral}
:::

::: {.flowrow}
[[ETS]{.flowtitle}[today]{.flownote}]{.flownode .navy}
[[Level, slope, season]{.flowtitle}[same three parts]{.flownote}]{.flownode .teal}
[[$\alpha, \beta^*, \gamma$ fitted]{.flowtitle}[the data chooses]{.flownote}]{.flownode .teal}
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the most important slide in the lecture and it costs nothing to
deliver, because they did the work yesterday.

Yesterday's fifth model decomposed the series, forecast the seasonally adjusted
part with drift, forecast the seasonal part with a seasonal naive, and added
them back. Every one of those choices was made by a human, in advance, and
pinned.

ETS keeps the same three parts and replaces the pinning with estimation. Alpha,
beta-star and gamma are what "the data chooses" means concretely: how fast each
part is allowed to change.

That framing is what makes today's model feel like a step rather than a new
subject. It also sets up the honest expectation for Part E: learning the
weights is not guaranteed to beat pinning them well.
:::

# D. The ETS family {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #00C9A7)"}

Ch 8.4 to 8.6 · The taxonomy, and the search over it

## Three letters name the model

| | Error | Trend | Season |
|---|---|---|---|
| **N** = none | | no trend | no season |
| **A** = additive | additive | linear trend | additive |
| **Ad** = damped | | damped trend | |
| **M** = multiplicative | multiplicative | | multiplicative |

. . .

**ETS(A,N,N)** is simple exponential smoothing. **ETS(A,A,N)** is Holt.
**ETS(A,A,A)** is additive Holt-Winters. That is Parts A, B and C, renamed.

::: {.notes}
Do not teach this table row by row. Put it up, say what the three letters are,
and immediately spend the time on the line underneath, which is the payoff: the
three models they just watched get built all have names in this scheme.

Two error types, five trend types counting none and damped, three season types.
That is thirty combinations, of which a handful are unstable and get excluded.

The one thing worth saying about the error letter, because it is the least
intuitive: additive error means the noise is a fixed number of units, and
multiplicative error means it is a fixed percentage. On a series that grew by a
factor of eight, that distinction is not cosmetic.
:::

## The error term is what buys the intervals

Holt-Winters is a recipe for a point forecast. ETS wraps the same recipe in a
statistical model by saying where the randomness enters.

::: {.incremental}
- A model with an error term has a **likelihood**, so its fit has a number
- A number means models can be **compared**, which is the next slide
- It also means the model can generate **futures**, not just a line
- Those futures are the prediction intervals, computed rather than assumed
:::

. . .

::: {.cardbox .teal}
Yesterday intervals cost an assumption you had to defend. Here they fall out of
the model, and it emits quantiles directly.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the answer to "why not just use Holt-Winters and stop". The point
forecasts are identical. What the state space form adds is the error term, and
the error term is what turns a recipe into a model.

Connect it to yesterday explicitly, because it is the same argument from the
other side. Yesterday, to get an interval out of a seasonal naive, they had to
supply an assumption: Gaussian errors, or bootstrapped residuals, or conformal
calibration. Each one spent something.

ETS carries its own error distribution, so the interval is part of the model
rather than an add-on. That is exactly why Part E can score it on scaled CRPS
without a line of new plumbing.
:::

## AutoETS fits the candidates and picks with AICc

```{python}
#| fig-width: 9
# The winner is 0 by construction, so its bar has no length; the label says
# what the missing bar means rather than leaving it to read as a glitch.
selected_tag = next(iter(d_aicc))
P.metric_bars(
    {(f"{k}  selected" if k == selected_tag else k): v
     for k, v in d_aicc.items()},
    fmt="{:.0f}", figsize=(8.6, 4.2),
    title="AICc distance from the best model (0 = the winner)")
plt.show()
```

AICc is the fit penalized for the number of parameters. `AutoETS` fits the
candidates, computes this for each, and returns the smallest.

::: {.notes}
Every bar here is a real fit on the spine, and the axis is the distance from
the winner rather than the raw AICc, because the raw numbers are all near 4500
and the differences are what matter.

Read the shape of the chart, not the individual values. The gap between the
models with a seasonal letter and the models without one is enormous, which is
the same conclusion Day 1 reached from the ACF: on retail data, seasonality is
what discriminates. Trend barely moves the number at all.

Say what AICc is in one sentence and move on: it rewards fit and charges for
parameters, so a model has to earn its complexity. The correction term is for
small samples and is irrelevant at 441 observations.
:::

## What it picked has no trend term

```{python}
#| echo: false
print(f"selected      : {METHOD}")
print(f"alpha (level) : {ALPHA:.3f}")
print(f"gamma (season): {GAMMA:.3f}")
```

::: {.cardbox .coral}
Multiplicative error, **no trend state**, additive season. On a series that
grew by a factor of eight.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the slide that earns the segment, so give it room and let the room
react before explaining it.

The explanation is in the level equation from Part A. With alpha at 0.52, the
level takes a half-step towards every new observation, so it climbs perfectly
well on its own. A trend state would let the model extrapolate that climb, and
that is the part AICc rejected: two more parameters, and a slope that has to be
right twelve months out, for a fit improvement that did not pay for them.

Connect it to Part B's callout. This is what "damping loses on this series"
looked like from the other end: the search did not merely damp the trend, it
removed it.

The lesson worth naming: an automatic search optimizes the criterion you gave
it, not the story you had in your head. It is not a substitute for looking.
:::

## The states it learned, read like a decomposition

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
P.decomposition_plot(
    states, ["level", "season"],
    title="The two states ETS fitted, month by month",
    ylabel="turnover ($M)", panel_height=2.3)
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Deliberately the same picture Day 1 drew with STL, in the same panel
vocabulary, because the point is that these are the same kind of object.

The level panel is the trend, arrived at without a trend state. The season
panel is the answer to the promise made two slides back: the seasonal state
starts at plus or minus a couple of units in 1982 and reaches plus 55 by 2018.

That growth is the multiplicative behaviour, showing up inside an additive
seasonal state. The model is coping with it through the multiplicative error
term, which is the next slide's subject.

If anyone asks why the season panel is so much noisier late in the series: the
swings are bigger in absolute terms, so a fixed percentage of noise is a bigger
number. Same reason.
:::

## Box-Cox does the same job as a multiplicative error

$$w_t = \begin{cases} \log(y_t) & \lambda = 0 \\ (y_t^{\lambda}-1)/\lambda & \lambda \neq 0\end{cases}$$

On the spine $\lambda \approx 0.074$, which is close enough to zero that it is
nearly the log transform Day 1 used.

. . .

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Transform the data**

Forecast on the stable scale, then transform back. Additive model, honest
intervals after back-transformation.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Or let the model do it**

A multiplicative error is already working on a relative scale. This is what
`AutoETS` chose here.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Box-Cox is one knob that spans the transforms they already know: lambda of 1 is
no transform, lambda of 0 is the log, and values in between interpolate. The
lambda that stabilizes the spine's variance is 0.074, which is why Day 1's log
transform worked as well as it did.

The columns are the honest summary of the choice. Both routes handle variance
that grows with the level. Transforming is more explicit and leaves you owning
the back-transformation. Letting the error term be multiplicative is one letter
in the model name.

Do not present either as correct. Present them as the same idea entering the
model at two different points, and note that this course took the second route
by accident, because it let the search choose.
:::

# E. Scoring it on the Day 2 harness {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #FF7A5C)"}

Ch 8.7 · The Day 2 harness, pointed somewhere new

## The harness takes it unchanged

```python
# The only new line is the model on line 4. Everything else is Exercise 2.5.
from coursekit import scoring

sf = StatsForecast(models=[AutoETS(season_length=12)], freq="MS")
cv = sf.cross_validation(df=spine, h=12, step_size=12, n_windows=8,
                         level=scoring.LEVELS)
scoring.score_cv(cv, "AutoETS", spine)     # mase, rmsse, crps, coverage_80
```

. . .

Nothing here is new except the model. Same folds, same metrics, same numbers
out.

::: {.notes}
Five lines, and four of them are yesterday's. Make that visible by walking the
code: the cross-validation call is the one they wrote in Exercise 2.5, with the
same h, the same step size, the same eight windows, and score_cv is the scoring
they did by hand there, packaged.

The only new thing is the model on line 4. That is what a harness is for, and
it is worth naming, because this afternoon a framework will do the same job
with a different API and they should be able to see what it is buying.

Say what happens if a model has no closed-form interval, since they will hit it
in the capstone: cross-validation refuses to score levels and asks for
prediction intervals. Conformal, from yesterday's segment E. ETS does not need
it.
:::

## One window flattered ETS. Eight folds do not

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
P.single_vs_cv_plot(
    single_mase, per_window[DAY3], labels=LABELS,
    figsize=(10, 3.4), log_right=False,
    titles=("One window against eight", "MASE, fold by fold"))
plt.show()
```

::: {.cardbox .navy}
On one window ETS scored `{python} f"{single_mase['AutoETS']:.2f}"` against
`{python} f"{single_mase['SeasonalNaive']:.2f}"`. Over eight folds the gap
closes to `{python} f"{mase['AutoETS']:.3f}"` against
`{python} f"{mase['SeasonalNaive']:.3f}"`, inside a fold spread of
`{python} f"{score['AutoETS']['mase_min']:.2f}"` to
`{python} f"{score['AutoETS']['mase_max']:.2f}"`.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is Exercise 2.4 and 2.5 happening again, to a different model, and it is
worth saying so out loud before explaining the chart.

Left panel. On the single 24-month window ETS scores 0.97 against the seasonal
naive's 1.11, which is a 13 percent improvement and the kind of number that
gets a model shipped. Over eight folds both lines land on 1.18 and the win
evaporates. Yesterday the decomposition route did exactly this, in exactly this
direction, on this same series.

Right panel is why. The fold-to-fold spread runs from about 0.72 to about 2.02
for both models, so a 0.007 difference in the means is a small fraction of the
difference between a good year and a bad one.

If someone asks whether the win is real, the honest answer is that eight folds
cannot settle a gap this size, and the next move is more folds or more series,
not a louder claim. That is why score_cv returns mase_min and mase_max.
:::

## And it loses the distribution

```{python}
#| fig-width: 9
# Five points, not the default ten: at ten, 87.5% would colour as honest and
# the chart would contradict the slide.
P.coverage_bars({LABELS[m]: cover80[m] for m in DAY3}, nominal=0.8,
                tolerance=0.05, figsize=(8.6, 2.8),
                title="Measured 80% coverage over 8 folds")
plt.show()
```

::: {.cardbox .coral}
ETS covers `{python} P.pct_label(cover80['AutoETS'])` of the holdout points with
a band that claims 80%. The seasonal naive covers
`{python} P.pct_label(cover80['SeasonalNaive'])`.
:::

::: {.notes}
Both bars miss, in opposite directions, and the ETS miss is the interesting
one because it looks like good news. The chart calls a band honest within five
points of nominal, which the seasonal naive clears and ETS does not.

Ask the room which model they would rather ship, before explaining. Most rooms
pick the 87.5 percent, because more coverage sounds safer. That instinct is
what the next slide takes apart.

A band that claims 80 and delivers 87.5 is not conservative, it is wrong by 7.5
points, and it is wrong in the direction that costs money: it is too wide, so
every decision made from it is hedged more than the evidence requires.

Recall yesterday's rule while it is on screen: coverage checks a band, it
cannot rank two bands. To rank them you need a proper score.
:::

## Too wide is a cost, not safety

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
P.width_vs_crps_plot(
    {LABELS[m]: width80[m] for m in DAY3},
    {LABELS[m]: crps[m] for m in DAY3},
    coverage={LABELS[m]: cover80[m] for m in DAY3},
    figsize=(10, 3.9))
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Left panel, the sharpness: ETS is carrying the wider band. Right panel, the
proper score: it loses on scaled CRPS. Those two facts are the same fact.

This is exactly yesterday's STL comparison run in reverse, and it is worth
saying so. Yesterday the decomposition route had the narrowest bands and the
worst coverage and still lost on CRPS. Today ETS has the widest bands and the
most coverage and still loses on CRPS. Neither sharpness nor coverage ranks a
forecast on its own. CRPS does, because it scores the whole distribution
against what actually happened.

The seasonal naive is not on top here because it is clever. It is on top
because its band is roughly the right size and roughly in the right place.
:::

## The verdict: a tie on points, a loss on range

| | Seasonal naive | ETS |
|---|---|---|
| MASE | `{python} f"{mase['SeasonalNaive']:.3f}"` | **`{python} f"{mase['AutoETS']:.3f}"`** |
| Scaled CRPS | **`{python} f"{crps['SeasonalNaive']:.4f}"`** | `{python} f"{crps['AutoETS']:.4f}"` |
| 80% coverage | `{python} P.pct_label(cover80['SeasonalNaive'])` | `{python} P.pct_label(cover80['AutoETS'])` |

. . .

::: {.callout-important}
## What to report
A fitted, selected, likelihood-based model matched a seasonal naive on the point
forecast and priced its uncertainty worse. That is the result. Report it.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is where a lot of forecasting projects quietly go wrong, so make the point
directly. A team that only tracked MASE would ship ETS today and write in the
summary that the new model beat the benchmark.

They would be reporting a 0.6 percent point-forecast improvement while shipping
intervals that are seven points too wide, and every downstream decision sized
off those intervals would be more conservative than the data justifies.

The floor holding is not a failure of the day. It is the strongest evidence
this course can offer that benchmarks are not a formality. A seasonal naive
took one line, took no fitting time, and is still the best-calibrated model in
the room.

Then hand over to the lab, where they do the whole thing themselves.
:::
